correctness.rationale: The nested expansion is a telescoping sum with total absolute increment 1−e^(−a); Haar integration and the character integral on each ball give the stated mass and conductor tails. The positive-coefficient expansion is absolutely summable over all characters (their sum is F_a(0)=1), so spectral testing captures finite-set positivity. An independent way to check the strict ratio ordering is to write Δ_a(j)/Δ_b(j) as (a/b) times the average of e^(−(a−b)t) with positive weight e^(−bt) on [p^(−j),p^(1−j)]. These successive intervals are ordered and disjoint except for endpoints. Thus these ratios tend strictly monotonically to a/b, and removing the first term of each positive weighted tail gives the same ordering for c_a(n)/c_b(n). Since c_a(1)=m_a−e^(−a) and e^a m_a strictly increases, the Haar ratio lies below the whole tail for a>b and above it for a<b. Averaging over p^NG preserves levels 0 through N; the unnormalized full finite Gram eigenvalues are p^N times the coefficients there. Hence the endpoint nullity is 1 or p^N−p^(N−1), respectively, with all modes zero for a=b at λ=1. Expanding each increment through t² and summing weighted terms reproduces the p^(−2N) and p^(−3N) terms of c_{p,a}(N), and division gives the stated p^(−N) excess. At the infinite endpoint for a<b, every coefficient stays positive: the limiting ratio is not attained by a single mode. For a>b only the constant is absent. A finite atomic measure killing all nonconstant characters would be a multiple of nonatomic Haar measure by Fourier uniqueness, so the kernel is still strictly positive definite on distinct sites. The RKHS contains every character with positive coefficient; character polynomial density gives all of C(G), or its closed Haar-mean-zero subspace if only the constant is absent.
residual_risks: The finite calculations are illustrative; infinite positivity and endpoint approximation rely on the analytic argument. Finite-depth claims require the stated coset averages, not point sampling with an unaveraged diagonal.

value.rationale: The Fourier cutoff is a natural quantitative test for subtracting one covariance profile from another. The same exact benchmark distinguishes finite-depth spectral degeneracy, infinite finite-set strictness, and uniform RKHS density, which are not interchangeable. When a<b, the depth-dependent gap and rank loss show explicitly why a coarse quotient can certify positivity at a subtraction level the compact group cannot support. This is a useful structural result beyond re-diagonalizing a single radial kernel.
residual_risks: Does not determine cutoffs for arbitrary profiles, metrics, or finite sampling conventions.
